analysis.one_liner: Bans credit bureaus from selling mortgage 'trigger leads' that alert lenders to shop for your loan.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it died in the House Financial Services Committee with zero cosponsors after being introduced January 30, 2020.
analysis.plain_summary: When you apply for a mortgage, your credit inquiry is recorded. Credit bureaus sell that inquiry as a 'trigger lead' to other mortgage lenders, who then call you — often repeatedly — pretending to have news about your own application. This bill would have changed federal credit reporting law to prohibit that: no credit bureau could sell your report based on a mortgage shopping inquiry you didn't initiate. It was introduced late in the 116th Congress and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it stayed until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People shopping for a home loan, who would stop getting unsolicited calls and emails from competing lenders who bought their credit information. Borrowers could shop rates on their own terms without their inquiries broadcasting their plans. Less pressure from competing lenders could also reduce the chance of borrowers being steered into loans.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that no consumer reporting agency may furnish a credit report for a transaction the consumer did not initiate, when the report is triggered by a residential mortgage inquiry [S3].
Trigger leads are the practice that lets other mortgage lenders know a consumer is shopping for a home loan; the bill would stop the creation and sale of those leads [S2].
The subjects include right of privacy and consumer credit, consistent with the bill's aim of stopping mortgage shoppers' credit information from being sold without their initiation [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus and the mortgage marketing industry, which earn revenue selling and reselling trigger leads. Mortgage lenders that rely on buying these leads to solicit borrowers would lose a customer acquisition channel and would have to win business through rates, service, or their own marketing.

drawbacks.text: Some competing lenders use trigger leads to reach borrowers who might otherwise pay a higher rate; banning them removes a channel through which borrowers can receive competing offers, and the burden of shopping for a better rate falls back entirely on the borrower.

The bill is narrow: it addresses only mortgage-related trigger leads, leaving the sale of trigger leads for other types of credit (auto loans, credit cards, personal loans) untouched, so consumers shopping for anything other than a mortgage get no protection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to borrowers — fewer unwanted solicitations that exploit data they never agreed to sell — is clear, and the cost is borne by companies whose business model depends on that data sale rather than by the public. The main honest objection is that trigger leads sometimes deliver competing offers that save borrowers money, and this bill would have removed that channel rather than, for example, requiring consumer opt-in. It was also a one-paragraph bill with no enforcement details or broader credit-reporting privacy reforms attached.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay introduced the bill in the House on January 30, 2020, near the end of the two-year Congress [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which was its only committee action [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
There is no record of a hearing, a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and mortgage lead sellers are better off, because the data sale the bill targeted continues. Lenders that buy trigger leads keep a channel for reaching borrowers who are actively shopping for a loan.

for.name: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban the sale of mortgage trigger leads; it received no cosponsors

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 30, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no vote or hearing ever held, the record shows no evidence of either party taking a position on the bill.

industries.industry: Consumer credit bureaus and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: Credit bureaus earn revenue by furnishing credit reports, including reports sold as trigger leads when a consumer shops for a mortgage. The bill would have barred that sale for mortgage inquiries, cutting off a data product these agencies sell to lenders and marketers [S3].

industries.industry: Mortgage lead brokers and marketing firms
industries.note: Lead brokers and marketing companies buy trigger leads from credit bureaus and resell them to lenders, which fuels the unsolicited calls borrowers get after applying for a mortgage. Banning trigger leads removes the product they sell [S2].

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders that purchase trigger leads
industries.note: Lenders that buy leads lose a way to find customers who are actively mortgage shopping; lenders that don't buy leads would face less poaching of their applicants mid-process. Borrowers would get fewer competing solicitations, which some lenders argue cuts both ways.
